planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early spring or fall, giving roots time to establish before summer heat or winter freeze.

directions: Site this compact, early-coloring red maple in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and water deeply during the first two seasons to encourage a strong root system. Its dense oval crown and reliably early scarlet fall display make it a good choice for smaller residential lots where the larger species types would crowd the space. Avoid highly alkaline soils, which can trigger chlorosis, and mulch to keep surface roots cool and moist. Little pruning is needed beyond removing crossing or damaged branches in the tree's dormant season.

planting.note: Transplant in spring or early fall into a site with room for a broad, dense crown.

directions: Brandywine is prized as a fruitless, low-litter red maple selection with sustained deep burgundy-red fall color that persists longer than many seedling red maples. Give it moist, well-drained soil and consistent watering while young; established trees tolerate periodic wet sites better than most maples but still perform best with even moisture. Because it produces little to no seed, it is a good low-maintenance choice for street and lawn plantings. Prune only to establish a strong central leader and remove weak crotches while the tree is young.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog

planting.note: Set out container or B&B stock in cooler spring or fall weather to reduce transplant stress.

directions: Sun Valley was bred for a tight branching structure and strong resistance to leafhopper damage, making it a durable pick for street tree plantings and parking-lot medians. Provide full sun and consistent moisture during establishment; once rooted in, it handles heat and moderately compacted urban soils better than many red maple selections. Its symmetrical, upright-oval form needs minimal corrective pruning beyond removing occasional water sprouts. Fall color runs a dependable orange-red on a slightly later schedule than the earliest-coloring cultivars.

planting.note: Plant in early spring or fall in a site large enough for a full-sized shade canopy.

directions: This selection was developed as an improved sport of October Glory, holding its rich red fall color for a longer window and coloring slightly earlier in the season. It grows best in full sun on evenly moist, well-drained soil, and adapts to both clay and sandy loam once established. Because it forms a dense, rounded crown, allow adequate overhead and root space away from structures and pavement. Water deeply during the first two growing seasons and apply a layer of mulch to conserve soil moisture and moderate root-zone temperature.

planting.note: Transplant in spring for best establishment, since sugar maples resent fall root disturbance in colder zones.

directions: Green Mountain was selected for its thick, leathery leaves that resist heat scorch and leaf tatter, making it noticeably more tolerant of urban and drought-prone conditions than typical sugar maple seedlings. Plant it in deep, well-drained soil and water regularly through its first few summers, since sugar maples are sensitive to soil compaction and root disturbance. Its dense oval-to-rounded canopy provides excellent shade and turns a strong orange-to-red in fall. Avoid sites with reflected heat or heavy road salt exposure, which will stress even this tougher selection.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog

planting.note: Set out in spring into deep, fertile soil with room for a large mature canopy.

directions: Legacy is a vigorous, fast-growing sugar maple selection noted for glossy dark green summer foliage and excellent heat and drought tolerance compared with straight-species seedlings. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and water consistently during the establishment period, then taper off once the root system is deep and wide. Its symmetrical, dense crown makes it a popular shade and street tree, and its orange-to-red fall display is dependable even in warmer parts of its hardiness range. Minimal pruning is needed beyond structural corrections while the tree is young.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

planting.note: Plant in spring for the strongest first-season root establishment.

directions: Fall Fiesta is valued for a sturdy, well-branched structure and glossy foliage that resists summer leaf scorch better than many sugar maple seedlings. It develops a vivid orange-to-red fall display and tends to color slightly later than earlier-turning cultivars, extending the autumn show. Grow it in full sun on rich, well-drained soil, watering deeply through establishment and avoiding compacted or poorly aerated planting sites. Its broad, rounded canopy makes it a strong choice for parks, campuses, and large residential lawns where its full mature size can be accommodated.

planting.note: Transplant in early spring into a site large enough for a full-canopy shade tree.

directions: Bonfire is a fast-growing sugar maple cultivar selected for a strong central leader and improved resistance to sun scald and frost cracking on the trunk, a common issue with young sugar maples in exposed sites. Plant it in full sun on deep, well-drained soil and keep the root zone consistently moist for the first two to three growing seasons. Its brilliant orange-red fall foliage and broad, uniform crown make it a popular shade tree for streets and open lawns. Wrap or shade the trunk of young trees in their first winters if planted in an exposed western or southern exposure.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog

planting.note: Set out in spring, giving the tree several years of consistent watering to establish its deep root system.

directions: Commemoration was selected for fast growth, glossy pest-resistant foliage, and reliably vivid orange-red fall color that develops earlier than many sugar maple seedlings. It performs best in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil and benefits from deep, infrequent watering rather than frequent shallow irrigation. The tree develops a dense, upright-oval canopy that provides strong shade while remaining well suited to lawn and park settings. Minimal pruning is required beyond early structural training to establish a single dominant leader.

planting.note: Plant in spring in a site with consistent moisture; birches establish poorly in dry or compacted soils.

directions: Whitespire is prized among ornamental birches for its bright white, non-exfoliating bark and notably better resistance to bronze birch borer than paper or European white birch. Give it consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, since birches are shallow-rooted and suffer quickly in drought or heat-stressed sites. It tolerates partial shade but develops the strongest bark color and form in full sun. Mulch generously to keep roots cool, and avoid heavy pruning in spring when sap flow is heaviest; prune in mid-summer or dormancy instead.

planting.note: Transplant in spring into deep, well-drained soil with room for a tall but narrow crown.

directions: This columnar tulip poplar selection retains the species' distinctive tulip-shaped flowers and yellow fall foliage but grows in a narrow, upright form well suited to streets and tight side-yard spaces where the straight species would be too wide. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and water consistently while the tree establishes its taproot. Its columnar branching is naturally strong, but young trees benefit from a single stake for the first year in windy sites. Avoid shallow or compacted soils, which stress this fast-growing tree's root system.

planting.note: Plant in spring in a location where its more compact mature size still allows for a substantial shade canopy.

directions: Developed at the University of Tennessee, this compact tulip poplar selection reaches roughly half the mature height and spread of the species while still producing the same showy orange-and-yellow tulip-shaped flowers. It grows best in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, though it tolerates light shade, particularly while young. Because it is markedly smaller than the straight species, it fits residential yards and smaller public spaces where a full-sized tulip poplar would eventually outgrow the site. Water deeply during dry spells in its first several years to support its rapid early growth.
sources: University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture

planting.note: Set out in spring in a site with room for a large mature canopy and some afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: This striking variegated tulip poplar carries a bright yellow-green margin on each leaf that fades to solid green as the season progresses, giving it a bicolor effect in spring and early summer. It prefers deep, moist, well-drained soil and benefits from light afternoon shade in hotter regions to prevent leaf-edge scorch on the variegated tissue. Watch for and prune out any reverted all-green shoots promptly, since they grow more vigorously and can overtake the variegated branches. Otherwise it is cultivated like the straight species, with deep watering during establishment and minimal routine pruning.

planting.note: Plant in spring into moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; tupelos resent being moved once established.

directions: Zydeco Twist is a distinctive black gum selection with contorted, twisting branches that give it strong winter and year-round sculptural interest beyond the species' usual fall color display. It tolerates both moist and average garden soils and adapts to wet sites better than most shade trees, making it useful near low spots or rain gardens. Grow in full sun for the best branch definition and fall color, though it tolerates partial shade, especially while young. Because of its irregular branching, little corrective pruning is needed or desired beyond removing dead wood.

planting.note: Transplant in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained soil, since tupelos have a taproot that resists later relocation.

directions: Green Gable is a uniformly pyramidal black gum selection with dense, glossy dark green summer foliage that turns dependable orange-red to purple in fall, making it a more predictable landscape choice than seedling-grown tupelos. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and provide supplemental water during establishment since this species develops a deep taproot that dislikes disturbance. It performs well in full sun to partial shade and tolerates occasional wet soils better than most shade trees. Once established it needs little maintenance beyond removing occasional dead or crossing branches.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog
